title: Xenophon Leads the Ten Thousand Home
text:
In 401 BC more than ten thousand Greek mercenaries marched deep into the Persian Empire for Cyrus the Younger, who was trying to overthrow his brother, King Artaxerxes. At Cunaxa, near Babylon, the Greeks won their part of the battle, but Cyrus was killed. They were stranded in the heart of a hostile empire, far from the sea.

Soon after, the Persian satrap Tissaphernes invited the Greek generals to a parley and had them seized and later executed. Xenophon, a young Athenian who had come along as a guest without any command, describes in his Anabasis how the army sank into despair that night. He could not sleep. He got up, called together the officers of his murdered friend Proxenus, and told them that waiting would mean death and that they must act at once and choose new leaders.

The army elected new generals, Xenophon among them. They burned their extra baggage, formed a hollow square, and fought their way north through the mountains of Kurdistan and the snows of Armenia. Months later, from a mountain, the vanguard saw the Black Sea and shouted "The sea! The sea!" Most of the army survived.
lesson: When the people in charge are gone and everyone is frozen, the one who speaks up with a plan becomes the leader.
location: From Cunaxa (modern Iraq) to Trapezus (modern Trabzon, Turkey)
caveat: Xenophon's account is the main source and naturally presents his own role favorably.
